insoluble

/in-SOL-yuh-buhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insoluble means impossible to solve.

The strange medieval manuscript's cipher has defeated professional codebreakers for over a century, and many experts now believe the puzzle is simply insoluble.

Example

For three generations, two branches of the Alvarez family have argued over who rightfully inherited the lake cottage, and every lawyer who reads the tangled, contradictory will declares the dispute insoluble.

The will is so contradictory that no reading of it can settle who owns the cottage, meaning the dispute has no possible solution. A problem or dispute with no solution to be found is exactly what insoluble describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unsolvable: Unsolvable means exactly what it says: no solution exists to be found. It is the plain-English twin of insoluble, and in most sentences the two are interchangeable. Insoluble is the more formal, test-favored word, the one writers reach for with grand problems like an insoluble paradox.

unanswerable: Unanswerable applies to questions: an unanswerable question has no answer that can ever settle it. Insoluble applies to problems, puzzles, and disputes, things that demand a solution rather than an answer. A riddle with no answer is unanswerable; a conflict no proposal can fix is insoluble.

irresolvable: Irresolvable describes a disagreement or conflict that cannot be settled between the people in it; an irresolvable feud grinds on because no compromise can end it. It needs parties and a standoff. Insoluble is wider, covering any problem or puzzle that has no solution at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

solvable: able to be solved

answerable: able to be answered or settled

Where it sits · how far beyond any fix it lies — tricky → insoluble → hopeless

tricky vs. insoluble: A tricky problem takes cleverness but can eventually be cracked; an insoluble one has no solution to find at all.

hopeless vs. insoluble: Calling a situation hopeless goes even further than insoluble, suggesting that nothing about it, not even the outlook, can ever improve.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not

Root — solu

Root — solu: to loosen, to solve (Latin solvere)

Suffix — -ble

Suffix — -ble: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: The prefix in- (not) plus the root solu (to loosen or solve) plus -ble (able to be) builds 'not able to be solved.' A knot that cannot be loosened is the perfect picture of an insoluble problem.

Use the root in a new word: resolve

Use the root in a new word: resolve: After one honest conversation, the roommates managed to resolve their long-running disagreement about chores.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / academic

Insoluble describes a problem, dispute, or puzzle that has no solution at all: an insoluble mystery, an insoluble conflict. Keep it distinct from intractable, which is broader and describes anything, including people and ongoing situations, that resists being managed or controlled even if a solution might exist somewhere. Insoluble also has a chemistry sense, 'unable to be dissolved,' but on the SAT the unsolvable-problem sense is the one to know.
